newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian political elite driven to act by scandals.
newsitem.headline: Belgian political elite driven to act by scandals.

text.p: Belgium's political elite, accused by public opinion of corruption and incompetence in dealing with a child sex and murder scandal, are making a last ditch attempt to prevent the government system collapsing.

Facing daily proof of bungled investigations into a series of child disappearances that led to the arrest in August of convicted rapist Marc Dutroux, the president of parliament has called a summit of party leaders.

"Politicians must answer the signals from the public. We are living in very extraordinary times. There is a crisis in the system and something must really be done," parliamentary president Raymond Langendries told Belgian media.

But less than a week before parliament is due to decide whether to send Francophone socialist Deputy Prime Minister Elio Di Rupo to court over allegations that he had sex with under-age boys, the call has received a mixed response.
Di Rupo denies the allegations. Belgian media have seriously questioned the reliability of the sole witness and some senior politicians have talked of political machinations.
The country's Francophone parties are largely in favour of the meeting, slated to take place at the weekend, but the Flemish parties are prevaricating.
Belgium's coalition government is made up of the Flemish and Francophone christian democratic and socialist parties.
"We need change...Our country is at war," Louis Michel, leader of the opposition Francophone Liberal Party told Belgian television.
But Herman de Croo, leader of the Flemish Liberal Party and the person who made the biggest public outcry over the allegations against Di Rupo, refused to be bound by any outcome.
In reality, political leaders have little choice.

In October some 250,000 people jammed the streets of Brussels in a demonstration of support for the parents of two young girls rescued from Dutroux's house, four others who were found dead and at least seven others still missing.
But the march also turned into a demonstration of disgust at a political and legal system widely seen as rotten to the core.

Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene promised rapid change but the evidence of incompetence and suspicions of worse now coming out at a parliamentary inquiry into earlier Dutroux investigations have raised the temperature still further.

In recent days parliamentarians have heard witnesses from the judiciary, who were involved in the hunt for missing girls, swear they had never even heard of Dutroux despite the fact that the gendarmerie had copious files on his activities.
Dutroux was released on parole in 1992 from a 13-year jail sentence for a series of rapes, some involving children.

Despite his record, the fact that he owned six houses although he had no visible means of support, that one witness swore he had been offered 150,000 francs ($5,000) by Dutroux to kidnap a child and the gendarmerie ran a surveillance operation against him for two years, magistrates say they knew nothing.
Investigators who visited Dutroux at home in December last year in connection with car thefts were not informed of his child sex past and made no link when they heard childrens' voices in the house.
It was later established that eight-year-olds Julie Lejeune and Melissa Russo were being held in the house at the time.
When Dutroux was later imprisoned for car theft, authorities turned off the water supply to the house.
Julie and Melissa were found in August, having starved to death while Dutroux was in jail.
